name: Founder-led store — understand what is happening
size:
AI analytics for small e-commerce stores
One primary storefront, a limited catalogue and a small set of data sources; low data volume need not mean simple operations.
quality: Order and product IDs may be usable while costs, refunds and campaign tags are incomplete. Start with reconciled reporting; short history limits reliable forecasting.
controls: Owner-controlled access, daily summaries and clear data timestamps. Restrict personal data; show the source behind answers before taking action.
roles: Founder or e-commerce owner buys and uses the tool; needs answers without assembling spreadsheets.
One generalist runs marketing, merchandising and customer operations; separate departments are not assumed.
No dedicated analyst required for basic reporting; a named business owner still validates metric definitions and recommendations.
departments: Orders plus ad spend → daily performance summary and unusual-change flags → owner reviews next steps. Platform ROAS is not proof of incremental sales.
Orders by product/variant → identify best sellers and weak sellers → choose a merchandising investigation.
Repeat-order history → simple returning-customer cohorts when sufficient records exist; avoid premature lifetime-value predictions.
Stock and recent sales, if available → low-stock checks → owner reviews replenishment needs.
Orders, refunds and supplied costs → provisional margin view. Missing costs must be visible, not filled with invented values.
Order status and authorised support records, if connected → summarise recurring queries; keep customer outreach under human review.
models: For a one-off or seasonal catalogue: compare product sales over relevant periods; short history cannot establish seasonality.
technology: Shopify is in the proposed architecture; another storefront needs a verified connector and compatible order/product fields.
Meta Ads, Google Ads and Klaviyo are design inputs, not proof of shipped connectors. Verify scopes, account access and common dates.
Cost or stock spreadsheet may be the only operational source; supplier and finance sources are not yet in the architecture.
Native reports/spreadsheets are the current alternative. Proposed semantic layer and AI analyst should expose definitions and source freshness.
trigger: The founder repeatedly downloads reports, cannot explain a sales change, or needs a trustworthy daily business summary.

name: Paid-growth DTC brand — diagnose acquisition performance
size:
AI data platform for growing DTC brands
Multiple campaigns/channels and an expanding catalogue; growth spend and decision frequency matter more than headcount.
quality: Align spend, order, refund and campaign data; agree attribution windows, time zones and currencies. Identity gaps limit cross-channel conclusions.
controls: Growth lead reviews recommendations; record attribution assumptions. Ad-budget changes require explicit approval, supported write access and spending limits.
roles: Founder or head of growth owns the business case and budget.
Performance marketer, e-commerce manager and creative/agency partners need shared answers rather than disconnected platform reports.
Marketing analyst or capable generalist owns metric definitions and checks anomalies; engineering support is conditional on source complexity.
departments: Spend and order cohorts → investigate acquisition efficiency and creative/product differences → propose tests. Do not infer causation from correlations.
Product conversion and return patterns → prioritise product-page or assortment tests; funnel analysis requires tracked events.
Klaviyo engagement plus order history → compare new/repeat buyer cohorts and propose lifecycle tests with consent controls.
Stock availability plus campaign demand → flag campaigns promoting constrained products, where inventory is connected.
Ad cost, discounts, refunds and unit costs → estimate contribution by campaign/product with transparent missing-cost exclusions.
Support/return themes → propose explanations for conversion or repeat-purchase issues; ticket data requires an additional source.
models: Launch-led or fashion brands: connect campaign timing to product/variant sales and returns; simulation needs elasticity assumptions and a test plan.
Replenishable products: compare acquisition cohorts by later repeat purchases before proposing spend shifts.
technology: Shopify order, product and refund data; verify event coverage before promising checkout-funnel analysis.
Meta/Google campaign data and Klaviyo cohorts, with stable definitions and permissions. Proposed architecture names these sources.
Product cost, fulfilment and inventory feeds extend the current design; verify the available data before a profitability claim.
Current point tools and dashboards may remain; governed metrics feed proposed AI explanations and reviewer-approved Slack/task delivery.
trigger: Ad platforms disagree with store results, paid spend grows faster than insight, or an agency/client review needs a joined-up explanation.

name: Repeat-purchase brand — retention and customer economics
size:
AI analytics for repeat-purchase and subscription commerce
Customer history, repeat events and subscription activity matter more than company size; this context can overlap with a small or large brand.
quality: Need deduplicated customer IDs, consistent order/refund history and enough repeat behaviour. Subscription states and cancellations require separate data where applicable.
controls: Honour consent and access boundaries; aggregate where possible. Validate cohort definitions and predictive error before activating audiences or retention offers.
roles: Head of retention, CRM lead or founder owns the retention outcome; finance reviews economics.
Lifecycle marketer and customer-experience operators turn approved segments and recommendations into campaigns.
Analyst or data owner checks customer identity, cohort windows and model calibration; a model score is not a guaranteed outcome.
departments: Acquisition source plus later order behaviour → assess cohort quality; avoid rewarding low acquisition cost without downstream economics.
Products bought together and reorder patterns → propose bundles or replenishment tests, subject to margin and stock checks.
Customer/order/engagement history → observed repeat-rate cohorts; propose churn/LTV estimates only after readiness and validation checks.
Repeat demand and stock data → investigate availability gaps affecting replenishment; do not assume a subscription forecast model exists.
Subscription schedules and supplier lead times, if connected → proposed demand scenarios → purchasing review; optional capability.
Refunds, acquisition costs and fulfilment costs → cohort contribution and payback estimates, with explicit cost assumptions.
Ticket themes, cancellations and refunds → identify service-related retention hypotheses; recommendations need review before contacting customers.
models: Durable or infrequent-purchase goods: retention may mean accessories, service or referrals rather than frequent repurchase.
Consumables/subscriptions: distinguish cancelled, paused and delayed orders before proposing renewal or replenishment interventions.
technology: Store order/customer data plus subscription billing/events where relevant; subscription connectors are additional requirements.
Klaviyo engagement and authorised acquisition data support cohort analysis; account identity and consent must be checked.
Returns, service, cost and supplier sources are extensions, not established native integrations.
Existing CRM/CDP or BI models may hold trusted segments. Proposed AI layer should reuse definitions rather than silently redefine customer value.
trigger: Repeat purchases flatten, acquisition payback becomes unclear, subscriptions grow, or teams cannot connect service/campaign behaviour to retention.

name: Catalogue and inventory-led merchant — plan stock and purchasing
size:
AI analytics for inventory-heavy e-commerce
Many SKUs/variants, multiple suppliers or warehouses; a small team with a complex catalogue can fit this ICP.
quality: Need consistent SKU/location IDs, stock snapshots, receipts, returns and supplier lead times. Stockouts censor observed demand; sales are not always unconstrained demand.
controls: Inventory/planning staff approve recommendations; forecasts need backtesting and uncertainty ranges. Never place purchase orders from an unvalidated simulation.
roles: Operations leader, merchandising head or owner sponsors the system.
Inventory planner, merchandiser and purchasing manager need different decisions from shared product data; roles may be combined.
Data steward validates inventory movements, costs and supplier mappings; an analyst tests forecast quality where prediction is proposed.
departments: Campaign plans plus available stock → flag potential conflicts and propose promotion changes for review.
Product/variant sales and returns → assortment comparisons → scenario analysis for range or price changes, only with explicit assumptions.
Purchase history plus availability → propose relevant cross-sell or replenishment audiences; consent and stock rules apply.
SKU/location movement → stockout/overstock investigation → proposed demand forecasts and safety-stock scenarios after validation.
Sales, purchase orders, lead times and minimum order quantities → compare replenishment options → buyer approves any order.
Costs, discounts, returns and stock balances → working-capital and margin scenarios; not an accounting valuation without agreed rules.
Delivery/return reasons plus product data → investigate service problems associated with specific variants or stock decisions.
models: Apparel/home goods: size/colour variants, launches and seasonal markdown decisions change the workflow.
Consumables: shelf-life/batch or subscription inputs may change replenishment; add those sources only where relevant.
Multi-location fulfilment: availability by warehouse/channel matters; transfers and reservations need explicit definitions.
technology: Store catalogue and order lines are starting points; SKU and variant identifiers must match operational systems.
Ad/lifecycle sources explain commercial context but cannot replace inventory and purchasing records.
OMS/WMS/ERP, purchasing and supplier feeds are necessary extensions for these use cases; current architecture does not prove them.
Existing inventory reports/BI provide baselines. Modelled data and a reviewed AI layer can be proposed above them; validate forecast and write-back support.
trigger: Persistent stockouts and dead stock, rising purchasing effort, catalogue expansion, or a need to understand demand before committing cash.

name: Omnichannel retailer — reconcile channels and locations
size:
AI data platform for omnichannel retail
Online store plus marketplaces, stores/POS or wholesale; location/channel complexity can appear before enterprise scale.
quality: Reconcile product/customer/channel IDs, returns, discounts, currencies and settlement dates. Online attribution does not automatically explain offline purchases.
controls: Role- and location-scoped access; show which channels are complete and current. Any price, stock or campaign change needs the appropriate channel owner's approval.
roles: Head of e-commerce, retail/operations leader or finance sponsor needs a consistent commercial view.
Channel managers, store operations, merchandising and finance consume different cuts of the same underlying data.
Analyst/integration owner governs cross-channel mappings and reconciliation; identity matching must respect permission boundaries.
departments: Cross-channel sales and media data → identify patterns worth testing; separate observed attribution from incremental impact.
Product performance by store/channel → range and price comparisons; account for returns, availability and channel-specific costs.
Consented customer identity across channels → cohort analysis where matching is legitimate and reliable; do not assume universal customer stitching.
Inventory by channel/location → availability discrepancies and allocation scenarios → operations review.
Supplier commitments plus channel demand → purchasing scenarios; avoid double-counting transfers or marketplace orders.
Orders, fees, settlements and refunds → channel profitability/reconciliation views when source coverage is complete.
Service records plus shipment/order data → investigate channel-specific issues; marketplace messaging permissions may restrict actions.
models: Seasonal categories: compare range and promotions by channel, with comparable calendars.
Repeat-purchase retail: reconcile loyalty and repeat behaviour only across permitted linked identities.
POS/marketplace/wholesale: each adds different order, return and settlement semantics; not merely another ad account.
technology: Shopify plus POS/marketplace/wholesale sources where used; non-Shopify connectors must be validated rather than assumed.
Advertising/lifecycle data may cover only some channels; expose those limits in reports and AI answers.
OMS/WMS, payments and accounting data connect orders to stock and economics; access and reconciliation rules are requirements.
Current channel dashboards or warehouse: agree canonical metric definitions; proposed AI recommendations should link to channel-specific supporting data.
trigger: Launching a new sales channel, conflicting channel totals, fragmented stock visibility, or margin decisions made from incomplete revenue reports.

name: Multi-brand business with a data team — governed AI decision support
size:
AI analytics for multi-brand / enterprise commerce
Several brands, entities, stores or regions, often with an existing warehouse. Data-team maturity is separate from revenue or employee count.
quality: Curated and raw datasets can coexist; semantic conflicts, lineage gaps and delayed feeds still need checks. Validated datasets, not unrestricted source access, should ground answers.
controls: Brand/role isolation, query budgets, audit trails and freshness rules. Predictive models require validation; write-back needs approved scopes, limits and accountable owners.
roles: Chief data/digital officer, group e-commerce lead or business sponsor defines scope and outcomes.
Specialist growth, CRM, merchandising, supply-chain and finance teams use domain-specific workflows.
Analytics engineers, analysts and security/data owners govern models, permissions and evaluation of AI answers.
departments: Governed cross-brand performance → explanations and scenario proposals → accountable budget owners review changes.
Brand/category/product comparisons → proposed assortment or conversion experiments with consistent definitions.
Permitted brand-level cohorts → retention hypotheses and model evaluation; no automatic pooling of personal data across brands.
Multi-site stock/demand views → validated forecast and allocation scenarios; preserve entity and operational constraints.
Supplier/lead-time/cost inputs → purchasing scenarios with explicit constraints and uncertainty; procurement retains authority.
Entity/brand contribution and planning scenarios → finance review and reconciliation; distinguish management estimates from booked results.
Authorised support themes → cross-functional issue summaries and task routing; no unsupported autonomous refunds or policy changes.
models: Diverse product categories: retain their different seasonality, returns and merchandising logic rather than forcing one playbook.
Subscription and transactional brands: use different retention and revenue definitions within governed models.
International/multi-entity operations: currency, calendars, permissions and source coverage are configuration requirements; not proof of global readiness.
technology: Several commerce platforms and brand accounts may feed approved warehouse models; named source support must be verified.
Multiple ad/CRM accounts require account ownership, permissions and consistent metric definitions.
ERP, warehouse, purchasing, fulfilment and support systems add business context where authorised; connector availability remains a validation task.
BigQuery/Snowflake or another warehouse and BI layer may already exist. Propose governed AI over trusted models; verify compatibility, latency and reviewer-approved activation.
trigger: An analytics request backlog, too many dashboards without decisions, inconsistent brand metrics, or a governed AI rollout over an existing data investment.
